constraint_review: Span 40 m; first vertical mode about 1.9 Hz — Met. The design uses a 40 m deck to size live load and places a transverse system at midspan for the first bending antinode, and tunes twin absorbers about 1.83 Hz off a 1.9 Hz primary with Den Hartog relations, so the stated span and frequency are the design inputs.
feedback:
Overall judgment: the working principle holds and the concept is buildable with ordinary steelwork and catalog dampers, so I would release it to detail design. Bridge motion at the midspan antinode drives two hanging masses through soft springs, the masses lag and viscous units turn relative motion into heat, and a friction-clamped cross beam returns the forces to the girders while the deck stays untouched. My biggest worries are the assumed 20 tonne modal mass, the use of a free-decay stroke for the stop gap, and the full stacked height versus girder depth, but none breaks the principle and margins look generous. Compared with the closest prior art, the MAURER retrofit twin TMDs under Zinggen Bridge in Brixen with two 240 kg half-mass packages on four coil springs in rib bays tuned to 2.45 Hz, this concept is different in support, tuning and verification because it uses one common 2.5 to 3.0 m transverse beam clamped with HSFG bolts carrying both 400 kg units, a detuned pair about 1.83 Hz for robustness, separate coil springs plus viscous dampers with caged stops and an 80 mm gap, and a Class III crowd acceptance to 0.67 m/s2 Medium.

Formulas and recomputation: I checked every deciding number against its physical relation. Modal stiffness follows k1 equals M times 2 pi f squared, and 20000 kg times 2 pi times 1.9 Hz squared gives 2.85e6 N per m which matches the 2.85e6 N per m on the board (E12). Mass ratio mu equals 800 kg divided by 20000 kg equals 0.04, so TMD mass 800 kg is correct for 4 percent (E13). Den Hartog tuning f2 equals f1 divided by 1 plus mu gives 1.9 Hz divided by 1.04 equals 1.83 Hz which matches the 1.83 Hz tuned frequency (E14). Optimum TMD damping ratio square root of 3 mu divided by 8 times 1 plus mu gives square root of 0.12 divided by 8.32 equals 0.12 or 12.0 percent which matches the board (E15). TMD stiffness k2 equals m times 2 pi f2 squared gives 800 kg times 11.5 rad per s squared equals about 1.05e5 N per m which matches the 1.05e5 N per m stiffness (E16), and damping c2 equals 2 zeta2 times square root of k2 m gives about 2.21e3 N s per m as used in the decay simulation (E17). Static sag delta equals m g divided by k2 gives 7848 N divided by 105000 N per m equals 0.0747 m or 74.7 mm which matches the sag (E63). Static weight 800 kg times 9.81 m per s squared equals 7.85 kN which matches the weight (E26). Live load 5 kN per m2 times 40 m times 3 m equals 600 kN which matches the live estimate (E30), so weight fraction 7.85 kN divided by 600 kN equals 1.31 percent is correct (E72) and total with 2.26 kN beam steel equals 10.11 kN divided by 600 kN equals 1.69 percent is correct (E76). Dynamic force m times omega squared times stroke gives 800 kg times 132.2 per s squared times 0.0494 m equals 5.22 kN which matches the dynamic load (E29). Slip resistance per bolt mu times preload divided by gamma gives 0.3 times 137000 N divided by 1.25 equals 32.9 kN which matches the capacity (E64), set against static plus dynamic 7.85 kN plus 5.22 kN equals 13.1 kN demand (E65). Stop force k times compression gives 105000 N per m times 0.08 m equals 8.4 kN which matches the stop hit (E66). Sag plus stroke 74.7 mm plus 49.4 mm equals 124 mm which matches the envelope (E68). Resonant acceleration follows a equals modal force per modal mass divided by 2 zeta, and equivalent synchronized pedestrians 5.92 times 280 N divided by 20000 kg gives 0.0828 m per s squared modal excitation (E42), divided by 0.01 gives 8.28 m per s squared bare (E43) and divided by 0.124 gives 0.67 m per s squared retrofitted at 6.2 percent effective damping (E44) (E45). Everyday scales support the regime: 8.28 m per s squared is about 0.84 g and 58 mm midspan motion which would indeed feel unsafe, 0.67 m per s squared is about 0.07 g which is noticeable but comfortable, 800 kg is about ten adults, 49.4 mm stroke is about two finger widths and 124 mm envelope is about a hand width, and 32.9 kN is about 3.3 tonnes.

Agreement and contradictions: sizes, counts and placements broadly agree with a single midspan transverse beam carrying two masses on springs with parallel dampers clamped to girders with stops and a midspan accelerometer (E55). I found measurable deviations that do not break function but must be recorded. The board at one place assumes 30 tonne modal mass (E9) and elsewhere 20 tonne (E12), and the design uses 20 tonne throughout; stiffness, mass and accelerations all depend on the 20 tonne choice. Weight fraction appears as 0.133 percent from mass over newtons (E71) and as 1.31 percent from kN over kN (E72), and the design correctly uses 1.31 percent. Demand 13.1 kN is static plus 5.22 kN dynamic without the 8.4 kN stop, while text says including stop hit; true static plus stop would be 7.85 kN plus 8.4 kN equals 16.25 kN, still below 32.9 kN per single bolt so margin remains about factor two. Tuning appears as 1.827 Hz in stiffness calc and 1.83 Hz in text, a rounding difference with no consequence.

Worst case of every limit: the comfort claim is shown for Class III 0.5 pedestrians per m2 or 60 people on 120 m2 with 5.92 synchronized (E40) (E41), not for denser Class IV, runners or vandals jumping, and the 80 mm gap is set against 49.4 mm stroke from a 20 mm free decay (E17) rather than a forced steady-state stroke at 0.67 m per s squared or a surge that hits stops. The stop and clamp still have margin because even static plus full stop 16.25 kN is half a single bolt capacity, and detuning sweeps hold 0.476 to 0.526 m per s squared (E70), but detail design should compute forced stroke and stop duty. Appearance is shown by nothing above deck and all hardware below soffit within girder depth in layout (E55), which satisfies without changing how the bridge looks from the deck at concept level.

Check 0, functions have means: capture bridge motion has the transverse cross beam moving with the antinode, supply counteracting force has the two tuned masses, dissipate energy has the paired viscous dampers, transfer loads has the HSFG clamp bolt set and beam, limit excess travel has the caged elastomer stop, maintain deck appearance has below-soffit placement with zero above-deck parts, and verify acceptance has the deck accelerometer array with logger and band assessor. No function is left without a part.

Check 1, sums against size and mass limits: added weight sums to 7.85 kN TMD plus 2.26 kN beam steel equals 10.11 kN against 600 kN live or 1.69 percent inside the assumed 2 percent rule, but housings, springs, dampers and stops beyond the 230 kg allowance are not itemized, so the sum is slightly incomplete though margin to 2 percent still allows about 1.9 kN or 190 kg. Vertical stack is not fully summed because mass height 300 to 600 mm plus spring 200 to 400 mm plus sag 74.7 mm plus stroke 49.4 mm could approach 500 to 1000 mm, argued only by envelope 124 mm and sketch showing fit within girder depth (E55) (E68); girder depth itself is not on the board, so fit is plausible for a 40 m span but not proven by addition.

Check 1b, numbered constraints computed: span 40 m is used in live load, frequency 1.9 Hz is used in tuning, weight fractions are computed, accelerations 8.28 and 0.67 m per s squared are computed against 0.5, 1.0 and 2.5 m per s squared bands, stroke 49.4 mm is computed against 80 mm gap, slip 32.9 kN is computed against 13.1 kN demand. All deciding quantities have a design value set against a limit.

Check 2, two values for same quantity: where two values appear I used the design value actually carried forward, namely 20 tonne modal mass not 30 tonne, 1.31 percent not 0.133 percent, 1.83 Hz nominal, and 13.1 kN nominal demand with note that stop-inclusive demand is 16.25 kN. Dependent calcs for stiffness, sag, force and acceleration all use the sourced design values except the noted stop inconsistency.

Check 3, flows traced end to end: vibration flows from main girders into the transverse beam clamped between webs, into coil springs and viscous dampers hung from the beam, into twin masses whose lag supplies inertia, with overtravel intercepted by stops; consecutive parts meet at the beam to spring, beam to damper, spring to mass and damper to mass joints as drawn. Signal flows from midspan accelerometer bolted at the antinode through wired logger to time record to comfort-band verdict with filed record. No step lacks a part and no gap is unbridged, and midspan transverse below-soffit placement is consistent throughout.

Check 4, open objections and meeting facts: the meeting closed by consensus after two cycles with all four members ready and no open objections, and the chief designer selections for suspension, tuning, damping, clamp, stops, concealment and acceptance are all supported by stated evidence. That consensus is consistent with the analysis above and I see no unsettled blocking point.

Evidence strength: comfort bands Maximum below 0.5, Medium 0.5 to 1.0, Minimum 1.0 to 2.5 and unacceptable above 2.5 m per s squared rest on a search result never opened (E19) and on simulation input (E45), and HSFG fatigue and preload rest on search results never opened (E24) (E25) (E57) (E58); they are weaker than page-read sources and decide comfort and clamp claims, so detail design should cite the opened Setra, HiVoSS or EN 1993 pages directly. Key claims resting on no board source are the 20 tonne modal mass, 3 m width and 0.5 percent bare damping inputs to force and acceleration; they are reasonable for a lively 40 m footbridge but need a modal mass and damping note or measurement plan. Remaining work for detail design, not for refusal, is to confirm modal mass and damping, run forced stroke at steady crowd resonance, sum full stacked height and masses including damper bodies, detail bolt count, edge distances and preload maintenance, and file the walk-through record; no bench test is required for concept acceptance.
